parts.text: Name 2 organisms that can be transmitted by aerosols, but are not thought to be transmitted person-to-person.
What would you expect serologies to be for a chronic coxiella infection.

cohort_answer.text: Redbook: Confirmation of persistent (chronic) Q fever is based on an increasing phase I IgG titer (typically ≥1:1024) that often is higher than the phase II IgG titer and an identifiable nidus of infection (eg, endocarditis, vascular infection, osteomyelitis, chronic hepatitis).

questions.question: You suspect an individual who presents with back pain with MRI findings of osteomyelitis/discitis has Q fever.

parts.text: What test would you order to diagnose and what values represent a positive test?
How would you treat this presentation?
Name of pathogen implicated in Q-fever

questions.model_answer:
a) Test: Coxiella burnetii phase I and phase II IgG serology (indirect immunofluorescence assay). A positive/chronic pattern is a phase I IgG titer ≥1:800 (phase I antibody exceeding phase II), consistent with chronic Q fever (in acute infection, phase II IgG predominates).
b) Three clinical manifestations of Q fever: (1) culture-negative endocarditis (chronic) (2) atypical pneumonia/self-limited febrile illness (acute) (3) hepatitis (acute) - vascular infection (aneurysm/graft infection) and osteoarticular infection (osteomyelitis/discitis) are additional chronic manifestations.
c) Treatment for chronic Q fever osteomyelitis/discitis: doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine for a prolonged course (typically at least 18 months, sometimes longer for bone/joint involvement).
d) Pathogen: Coxiella burnetii.

questions.question: Person exposed to farm animals and now has disciitis and osteomyelitis. You suspect Q fever.

parts.text: How to diagnose it? How would it look for an acute infection
What is the treatment regimen for this person

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Serology, PCR, biopsy. Acute infection: Phase 1 IgG (to diagnose osteomyelitis/endocarditis) would look lower than Phase 2 for acute infection - reverse true in chronic infection (rising phase 1 IgG titer higher than phase 2). Negative test in first week does not rule out Q fever. Phase 2 IgG: acute rise in acute/convalescent serology by 4-fold, or (per CDC) single positive IgG Phase 2 of >1:128; chronic >=1:800 (Major Duke Criteria). Syndromes: A self-limited flu-like illness; Pneumonia; Hepatitis. Treatment: Doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine for 18 months. Pathogen: Coxiella burnetii
